
Using Python to do a random forest classification

```{python}
# import libraries
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import os
```

```{python}
# import data with pandas
tg = pd.read_csv("../data/processed_grid/time_grid.csv")
tg.head()
```

The National Wildfire Coordinating Group (NWCG) has size classifications for wildfires ([link](https://www.nwcg.gov/node/1737420)). We may limit smaller fires (which may represent minor incidents and not actual wildfires), so adding a factor for this classification.

Class A - one-fourth acre or less;
Class B - more than one-fourth acre, but less than 10 acres;
Class C - 10 acres or more, but less than 100 acres;
Class D - 100 acres or more, but less than 300 acres;
Class E - 300 acres or more, but less than 1,000 acres;
Class F - 1,000 acres or more, but less than 5,000 acres;
Class G - 5,000 acres or more.

```{python}
# categorizing max_acres into class bins
bins = [0, 0.01, 0.25, 9.99, 99.99, 299.99, 999.99, 4999.99, 9000000]
labels = ["No fire", "Class A", "Class B", "Class C", "Class D", "Class E", "Class F", "Class G"]

tg['size_class'] = pd.cut(x = tg['max_acres'], bins = bins, labels = labels, include_lowest=True)
```

```{python}
# more libraries
# %pip install scikit-learn
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.model_selection import (
    train_test_split, cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold
)
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, roc_auc_score, r2_score, mean_squared_error

```

```{python}
# label encoder for target variable
label_encoder = LabelEncoder()
target = label_encoder.fit_transform(tg["size_class"])

data = tg[['is_ndgn', 'plnt_sm', 'rx_csum']]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    data, target, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)
```

```{python}
# random forest classifier with defaults
rf = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)

rf.fit(X_train, y_train)

pred = rf.predict(X_test)

print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test, pred):.4f}")
```

```{python}
# trying with rolling sum instead of cumulative
data_r = tg[['is_ndgn', 'plnt_sm', 'rx_rollsum']]

X_train_r, X_test_r, y_train_r, y_test_r = train_test_split(
    data_r, target, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)
```

```{python}
# random forest classifier with defaults
rf_r = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)

rf_r.fit(X_train_r, y_train_r)

pred_r = rf_r.predict(X_test_r)

print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test_r, pred_r):.4f}")
```

It's the same accuracy with a rolling sum instead of a cumulative sum which seems strange but I guess who am I to judge. 

Trying without plant sum. 

```{python}
# trying with rolling sum instead of cumulative
data_np = tg[['is_ndgn', 'rx_csum']]

X_train_np, X_test_np, y_train_np, y_test_np = train_test_split(
    data_np, target, test_size=0.3, random_state=42
)
```

```{python}
# random forest classifier with defaults
rf_np = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)

rf_np.fit(X_train_np, y_train_np)

pred_np = rf_np.predict(X_test_np)

print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy_score(y_test_np, pred_np):.4f}")
```

Looking at feature importance. 

```{python}
# %pip install shap
import shap
```

```{python}
explainer = shap.TreeExplainer(rf)
shap_values = explainer.shap_values(data)

# calculate mean absolute SHAP values
shap_summary = np.abs(shap_values).mean(axis=0)

# list to store shap values for each feature
shap_summary_list = [np.mean(shap_summary[i]) for i in range(shap_summary.shape[0])]

# list of feature names
feature_names = ['is_ndgn', 'plnt_sm', 'rx_csum']

# dataframe using 1d list of SHAP values
shap_summary_df = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': feature_names, 'SHAP values': shap_summary_list})

print(shap_summary_df)
```

Feature importance using Gini importance.

```{python}
# creating dataframe of gini importances
feature_imp_df = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': feature_names, 'Gini Importance': rf.feature_importances_})

print(feature_imp_df)
```

Feature importance for rolling sum of rx.

```{python}
feature_names_r = ['is_ndgn', 'plnt_sm', 'rx_rollsum']

# creating dataframe of gini importances
feature_imp_df_r = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': feature_names_r, 'Gini Importance': rf_r.feature_importances_})

print(feature_imp_df_r)
```

It appears that the rolling sum is worse! 

Feature importance without plant sum. 

```{python}
explainer_np = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_np)
shap_values_np = explainer_np.shap_values(data_np)

# calculate mean absolute SHAP values
shap_summary_np = np.abs(shap_values_np).mean(axis=0)

# list to store shap values for each feature
shap_summary_list_np = [np.mean(shap_summary_np[i]) for i in range(shap_summary_np.shape[0])]

# list of feature names
feature_names_np = ['is_ndgn', 'rx_csum']

# dataframe using 1d list of SHAP values
shap_summary_df_np = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': feature_names_np, 'SHAP values': shap_summary_list_np})

print(shap_summary_df_np)
```

Feature importance using Gini importance.

```{python}
# creating dataframe of gini importances
feature_imp_df_np = pd.DataFrame({'Feature': feature_names_np, 'Gini Importance': rf_np.feature_importances_})

print(feature_imp_df_np)
```

In this case, Gini importance and SHAP values do not align! Fascinating. What a world. I need to go to sleep it is now one in the morning.
